# Assalāyana Sutta (MN 93 (PTS MN ii 147))

**ID:** MN 93 (PTS MN ii 147)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Assalāyana Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Assalāyana
**PTS:** MN ii 147
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/mn93
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0202m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Assalāyana Sutta* (MN 93) is set at Sāvatthi in Jeta's Grove and articulates a foundational early Buddhist critique of caste hierarchy [Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Humphreys 1956; Holder 2006]. Five hundred brahmins encourage a sixteen-year-old prodigy, Assalāyana—well-versed in the three Vedas and traditional marks of a Great Person—to debate the Buddha and defend the claim that brahmins are the supreme, pure caste born from the mouth of Brahmā [SuttaCentral; Holder 2006; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995]. The Buddha refutes this doctrine through several empirical and ethical arguments: brahmin women visibly menstruate, become pregnant, and give birth like all other women [History of civilisation; Holder 2006]; karmic consequences for evil or virtuous deeds apply equally regardless of status [Holder 2006; Collins 1993, 2001]; and caste systems are merely contingent social customs, as in the frontier regions of the Yonas and Kambojas, where only two classes (master and slave) exist and can interchange [Collins 1993, 2001; Vassiliades].

A prominent passage cited extensively in later discussions of Buddhist embryology recounts an ancient dialogue establishing that conception requires three factors: the union of parents, the mother being in season, and the presence of a *gandhabba* (an entity seeking rebirth) [Wayman 1984; Cuevas; Langenberg; Anālayo 2018]. Because none can establish the caste of the incoming *gandhabba*, claims of hereditary purity collapse [Wayman 1984; Anālayo 2018].

Curated parallels include two Chinese translations in the *Madhyama-āgama* (MĀ 151) and the separate text T 71, along with *Ekottarika-āgama* 40.9 [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms these alignments with MĀ (ZH_T01_0026) and T 71 (ZH_T01_0071), alongside Tibetan textual parallels [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus identifies substantial shared text with other suttas critiquing caste, notably the *Madhura Sutta* (MN 84), *Esukārī Sutta* (MN 96), and *Aggañña Sutta* (DN 27) [DharmaNexus]. Complete English translations have been published by I.B. Horner, Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, and Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Wayman 1984].
